We don’t just look at the stars—we code for them. 🚀

We are Oribt Architect, a high-powered crew of hackers, designers, and space enthusiasts crashing into the NASA Space Apps Challenge. Armed with coffee, curiosity, and NASA’s open-source data, we are tackling Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars. Our mission? To turn complex cosmic data into a sleek, game-changing solution that leaves a mark on Earth and beyond. Fasten your seatbelts
summary:
Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is a browser-playable, first-person 3D survival game for kids aged 7–12 that turns the real trade-offs of running a lunar or Martian outpost into hands-on play. Players enter their name, choose an avatar and pick the Moon or Mars, then run an outpost with PIP, a friendly robot from Mission Control who talks to them by voice.
Each mission is built around a real constraint: shielding the crew from a solar storm, growing food, surviving an oxygen emergency and keeping communications alive across the light-time delay. No choice is free. Raising shields costs power, saving power costs food, and every decision adds to the crew's radiation dose. Wrong choices play out and are then explained, so failure teaches instead of punishing.
details:
Project Details *:

What exactly does it do?

The game puts a child in the role of a junior astronaut running an outpost. Across a series of missions the player balances power, life support (oxygen and food) and radiation shielding while real space conditions push back. It teaches the reasoning astronauts and mission planners actually use, not just facts about space.

• Personal and story-first: the player enters their name and picks an avatar, and PIP and the crew address them by name. A story intro teaches controls and tasks before play begins.

• Real consequences: every decision has a cost. Wrong choices play out, then PIP explains what happened and what real astronauts would do.

• Explore and unlock: a mission map with locked areas that open as missions are completed.

What benefits does it have?

• Teaches real engineering trade-offs, not just space trivia, at a level kids aged 7–12 can follow.

• Built on live and published NASA data, attributed inside the game, so the science is traceable and verifiable.

• Every playthrough is different because real space weather changes daily, which encourages replay.

• Failure is safe and explained; scientific terms such as sol, radiation dose and microgravity are explained in context.

What do we hope to achieve ?

We want children to develop a deeper understanding of what space exploration truly involves. Beyond rockets and astronauts, we want them to experience the importance of scientific thinking, problem-solving, teamwork, and resource management. By making mission-critical decisions and experiencing their consequences, children should understand that every choice matters when it comes to astronaut survival and mission success.

Tools, Technologies, Coding Languages, Hardware and Software Used

1. Technology Stack

Game Engine – Unity 6 (Universal Render Pipeline)

Used to develop 3D environments, scenes, physics, lighting, and interactive gameplay.

Programming Language – C#

Used to implement game logic, mission systems, resource management, radiation dose calculations, player decisions, and their consequences.

Web Build – Unity WebGL Export

Allows the 3D game to run directly in modern web browsers without requiring users to install the game.

Website Development – HTML, CSS, JavaScript

Used to build the solar-system landing page, live NASA data tickers, and information cards.

Data Proxy – PowerShell Server (serve.ps1)

Fetches NASA JPL Horizons data and makes it accessible to the browser, overcoming direct browser access restrictions caused by CORS.

2. Live APIs and External Data Sources

A. NASA and Space Weather Data

1. NASA DONKI (CCMC – api.nasa.gov)

- Data: Solar flare classifications and Coronal Mass Ejection (CME) speed.

- Used in game: Determines Moon 1 storm strength, Moon 2 CME warnings, Solar Plan cards, and Mars 2 storm events.

2. NOAA SWPC GOES

- Data: Solar X-rays, proton flux (10 MeV or higher), and Kp index.

- Used in game: Calculates today's radiation risk multiplier (×0.8 to ×1.6) and displays information on the communications desk screen.

3. NASA SDO / HMI

- Data: Solar images and sunspot observations.

- Used in game: Powers the Moon 2 telescope activity, where players identify real sunspots.

B. NASA and JPL Scientific Data

4. NASA JPL Horizons

- Data: Sun and Earth positions in the Moon's sky, Earth–Moon distance, and Earth–Mars distance.

- Used in game: Determines sunlight direction, powers the solar panel and dish systems, and calculates Moon 4 radio delay and Mars communication delays.

5. NASA EPIC / DSCOVR

- Data: Latest full-disc images of Earth.

- Used in game: Fetches real Earth imagery directly into the game.

6. NASA OSDR (Open Science Data Repository)

- Data: Plant growth studies conducted in space.

- Used in game: Supports the Moon 2 and Mars 2 "Real Space Plant Science" card, introducing players to actual plant research in space.

7. Curiosity REMS (mars.nasa.gov)

- Data: Mars surface temperature, atmospheric pressure, and sky conditions.

- Used in game: Powers the Mars weather station and Mars 3 flight card.

C. Space Exploration and Astronomy Data

8. NASA Deep Space Network (DSN) Now

- Data: Information about which spacecraft are communicating with Earth in real time.

- Used in game: Featured in Moon 1 and Moon 4 cards.

9. JPL CNEOS Close-Approach API

- Data: Asteroids passing near Earth.

- Used in game: Provides real-world asteroid information for the Moon 3 card.

10. JPL CNEOS Fireball API

- Data: Fireballs and meteors burning up in Earth's atmosphere.

- Used in game: Adds real-world meteoroid context to the Moon 3 card.

11. NASA APOD (Astronomy Picture of the Day)

- Data: Daily astronomy images and descriptions.

- Used in game: Available as an external data source; no specific in-game use is assigned.

12. NASA Images API

- Data: Searchable NASA image library.

- Used in game: Available for retrieving NASA imagery; no specific in-game use is assigned.

D. Live Space and General Information Sources

13. People in Space (corquaid JSON)

- Data: Information about who is currently in space.

- Used in game: Featured in Moon 2 and Moon 3.

14. WhereTheISS.at

- Data: Live International Space Station (ISS) position.

- Used in game: Featured in Moon 3.

15. Simple English Wikipedia

- Data: Easy-to-understand scientific and general knowledge.

- Used in game: Provides PIP, the in-game assistant, with accessible information for answering player questions.
